title: El Niño puts India on course for driest monsoon since 2009
excerpt: Rainfall is running 15% below the long-term average with less than two weeks left in the season, threatening crop yields and food prices in the world's biggest rice-producing country.
body:
• The India Meteorological Department says cumulative rainfall since June 1 is 15% below the long-term average; if the deficit holds, this will be the weakest monsoon since 2009, when rain finished 18% below normal.
  • Rice production could fall by around 10 million metric tons — a 6.5% drop from last year's record 154 million tons and the biggest decline in nearly two decades, the Rice Exporters Association says.
  • Food inflation climbed for a seventh straight month to 5.95% in August, its highest level this year; the government has allowed duty-free sugar imports and is selling subsidized onions in some states.
  • A possible Bay of Bengal cyclone in the last week of September could bring late rain to the east, but forecasters expect the season to end with a deficit of 13% to 16%.

A monsoon running dry

India is on course for its driest monsoon in 17 years as a strengthening El Niño chokes off rainfall across the subcontinent. Cumulative rainfall for the June-to-September season stands 15% below the long-term average, according to the India Meteorological Department — and with less than two weeks of the season left, the deficit would make this the weakest monsoon since 2009, when rain finished 18% below normal.

The figure has already blown past the weather office's own forecast. The IMD had projected just a 10% shortfall back in May.

Context & Background

The southwest monsoon delivers most of India's annual rainfall, and hundreds of millions of farmers depend on it to irrigate fields in a country that ranks among the world's biggest producers of rice, sugar and cotton. Food and beverages account for 36.75% of India's consumer price index, so a weak monsoon almost always shows up at the checkout counter. The last comparable failure — 2009, also an El Niño year — ended 18% below normal and curtailed rice output sharply.

Impact & Analysis

Food inflation is already accelerating, rising for a seventh straight month to 5.95% in August, its highest level this year. Yuvika Singhal, an economist at QuantEco, estimates that every one-percentage-point shortfall in monsoon rain typically raises food inflation by about 25 basis points.

Rice is taking the hardest hit. India harvested a record 154 million tons last year, and output could now fall by around 10 million metric tons, or 6.5% — the first decline in a decade and the biggest drop in nearly two decades, industry officials told Reuters. The area under summer-sown rice stood at 42.68 million hectares as of September 11, nearly 4% below a year earlier, and in some rice-growing states the rainfall deficit runs as high as 42%.

"Yields will be lower due to reduced rainfall. We estimate that production could decline by around 10 million metric tons."

— B.V. Krishna Rao, president of the Rice Exporters Association

The cushion is stock. State rice reserves, including unmilled paddy, totaled a record 59.6 million tons on September 1 — far above the government's 10.3-million-ton target for October 1 — so New Delhi can keep exports flowing without restrictions. Even so, local rice prices have started climbing, lifting export prices to their highest in more than a year. Plantings of sugarcane and corn are also running behind last season, and the government has allowed duty-free sugar imports while selling onions at subsidized prices in some states.

Not everyone is alarmed. Chief Economic Adviser V. Anantha Nageswaran said this week that food inflation, at roughly 6% in August, was unlikely to persist through year-end, calling the monsoon shortfall "manageable" and noting that summer crop sowing was only 2–3% below last year's level. But reservoir storage sits below last year's level and the ten-year average, and lower carry-over water could weigh on winter rabi sowing if autumn rains also disappoint.

Diaspora Angle

For the diaspora, the effects will arrive in two places: the grocery aisle and the remittance ledger. Higher export prices — already at a one-year high — tend to filter through to basmati and staple rice prices at Indian stores in the US, the UK and the Gulf, while rising food costs at home may prompt families to ask relatives abroad for help sooner, and for more.

What's Next

The final weeks will decide whether the season ends closer to 13% or 16% below normal. A forecasting platform at Lancaster University known as CRUCIAL assigns a 68% chance the deficit lands between 10% and 20%, according to founder Mark Roulston. Conditions may turn favorable for a tropical cyclone in the Bay of Bengal in the last week of September, said Christian Werner of consultancy Global Weather Climate Analytics — late rain that could ease the deficit in the east but is unlikely to change the national picture. Soil moisture and reservoir levels will decide the winter crop — and how long this monsoon's shadow lasts.

nri_angle: With rice export prices at their highest in more than a year, NRIs are likely to see Indian grocery bills climb abroad while families back home face rising food costs.
